verses.bibleText: If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The opening “If” does not express uncertainty about the Colossians’ relationship to Christ. It asks them to acknowledge the consequence of what has already occurred: through faith, confessed in baptism, they have been united with the crucified and risen Lord. Chapter 2 warned them against religious regulations, ascetic severity, angelic preoccupations, and visionary claims that appeared spiritual but could not conquer the flesh. Chapter 3 now gives the positive alternative. Spiritual life is not found by constructing a ladder from earth to heaven; it is received through union with Christ, who has already died, risen, ascended, and been enthroned.

To “seek those things which are above” is therefore to seek Christ Himself and to allow His heavenly reign to determine earthly conduct. Paul is not encouraging withdrawal from work, family, society, or bodily life. The remainder of the chapter deals directly with speech, sexuality, forgiveness, worship, marriage, children, parenting, and labor. Heavenly-mindedness is measured by Christlike faithfulness within those ordinary settings. What is “above” is the rule, character, truth, and hope associated with the exalted Lord; what must be rejected is the fallen order of selfish desire and humanly invented religion.

Christ’s place at the right hand of God recalls Psalm 110:1. It signifies honor, royal authority, victory over hostile powers, and participation in the divine government of the universe. The One whom the Colossian philosophy risked obscuring behind intermediaries is above every principality and power. Nothing can supplement His sufficiency or improve the believer’s access to God.

His sitting also testifies to the completed sufficiency of His once-for-all sacrifice. It does not imply inactivity. The enthroned Christ remains the living Lord who intercedes for His people, ministers on their behalf in heaven, nourishes His body, and directs His kingdom toward its appointed consummation. Christian ethics begin, therefore, neither with fear nor with self-improvement, but with the risen Christ and the new identity freely given in Him.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to be raised together with another. It describes the believer’s present participation in Christ’s resurrection life without eliminating the future bodily resurrection.
A present imperative calling for a continuing pursuit and settled orientation, not a momentary religious impulse.

verses.bibleText: Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The command of verse 1 is restated with greater emphasis on the inner orientation from which conduct proceeds. The KJV expression “set your affection” should not be limited to emotion. Paul is speaking about the mind’s governing disposition—the convictions, desires, values, and purposes by which a person interprets life and chooses a course of action. A Christ-centered life requires a continually renewed outlook because the old patterns of thought remain eager to reclaim their former influence.

“Things on the earth” cannot mean the created world as though matter, work, marriage, food, or the human body were inherently evil. Such an interpretation would resemble the ascetic error Paul has just rejected. God created the earth, Christ sustains it, and believers are called to serve faithfully within it. Earthly-mindedness is the outlook of the fallen age: self-exaltation, sensual appetite, greed, hostility, deceptive speech, social pride, and religion shaped by human rules rather than by Christ. These are precisely the matters addressed in verses 5-11.

To set the mind above is to view life from the reality of Christ’s throne. His authority becomes more decisive than social pressure; His approval matters more than human applause; His promised kingdom outweighs immediate advantage; and His character supplies the pattern for relationships. Such an outlook is not escapism. It sends the believer back into the world with purer motives, stronger hope, and a clearer sense of responsibility.

The contrast also exposes the irony of the false teaching. A system may speak constantly about visions, angels, mysteries, or heavenly ascent and yet remain thoroughly earthly if it separates people from Christ, encourages pride, or leaves sinful desire unconquered. True heavenly wisdom produces humility, holiness, love, peace, gratitude, and faithful service. The mind is genuinely fixed above when the life below begins to resemble the Lord who reigns there.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb concerns a settled disposition or governing outlook involving thought, desire, judgment, and will. It means more than entertaining occasional religious thoughts.

verses.bibleText: For ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The exhortation to seek heavenly things rests on a decisive change of allegiance: “ye are dead,” more precisely, “ye died.” Physical death is not in view. Through union with Christ, the believers have died to the former order in which sin, hostile powers, human traditions, and the fear of condemnation exercised dominion. Baptism bore public witness to this break, but the saving reality lies in faith’s union with Christ, not in an external ceremony considered apart from Him.

Dying with Christ does not mean that temptation has vanished or that the believer can no longer choose disobedience. The commands that follow would be unnecessary if sin had become impossible. It means that sin no longer possesses rightful lordship. The old life has received its judgment in the cross, and believers are now summoned to make that decisive reality visible in daily choices. They are not trying to die in order to become accepted; because they have been accepted in Christ, they are to refuse the conduct belonging to the life from which He has delivered them.

Their new life is “hid with Christ in God.” Its source, security, and final destiny lie beyond what the world can presently see. Outward circumstances may make Christians appear weak, obscure, or defeated. They remain subject to suffering, aging, and death, and the glory promised to them has not yet been publicly revealed. Nevertheless, their identity is real because it is joined to the living Christ.

Hiddenness also carries the thought of safekeeping. The believer’s hope is not preserved by human strength but entrusted to God in Christ. This security should produce confidence without presumption. The life hidden in God is a life of continuing dependence, faith, and obedience. Its invisibility does not make present conduct unimportant; rather, conduct is meant to bear quiet witness to the reality that will be fully disclosed when Christ appears.

wordNotes.explanation: The perfect tense describes an accomplished hiding whose result continues. The expression conveys both the present invisibility of the believer’s true identity and its security with Christ in God.

verses.bibleText:
When Christ,
who is our life, shall appear, then shall ye also appear with him in glory.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The hidden life of verse 3 moves toward public revelation. Christ is called “our life” because every dimension of salvation is bound to Him. He obtained life for His people through His death, communicates spiritual life through union with Himself, sustains that life in the present, and will complete it when He returns. Christianity is therefore more than receiving benefits from an absent benefactor. The believer’s life is inseparable from the living Lord.

Christ’s appearing refers to His visible return, not to an inward religious experience or a merely symbolic advance of the gospel. The One now hidden from mortal sight will be manifested in glory. His return will expose the false judgments of the present age: the rejected Christ will be revealed as universal Lord, and those whose lives seemed insignificant because they belonged to Him will be openly identified with His victory.

“Then shall ye also appear with him in glory” preserves the future dimension of salvation. Believers have been raised with Christ in the spiritual sense of entering newness of life, but they still await bodily resurrection and transformation. At His coming, the dead in Christ will be raised incorruptible, and the living faithful will be changed. Mortal bodies will be fashioned after the likeness of His glorious body. The hope is not an immortal soul enjoying its final reward apart from the body; it is the restoration of the whole person through resurrection at the appearing of Christ.

The words “with him” emphasize shared destiny rather than independent human immortality. Whatever glory the redeemed possess is derived from Christ and enjoyed in communion with Him. Their present life may be concealed by suffering, weakness, and death, but none of these can defeat the purpose secured in the risen Lord.

This expectation gives moral urgency to the chapter. Future glory is not offered as an excuse to neglect present faithfulness. Because believers expect to be revealed with Christ, they are to put away everything inconsistent with His character. Hope purifies conduct by drawing the heart toward the One who is coming.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to be manifested or made visible. Christ, presently unseen by the world, will be publicly revealed at His return.

wordNotes.term: our life — ἡ ζωὴ ἡμῶν (hē zōē hēmōn)
wordNotes.explanation: Christ is not merely the giver of life; He is its living source, controlling center, and guarantee of its future fulfillment.

verses.bibleText: Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The “therefore” joins moral action to the believer’s union with Christ. Those who have died with Him are commanded to put sinful practices to death. Grace does not make obedience unnecessary; it creates the new relationship in which obedience becomes both required and possible. The believer is not earning acceptance by defeating sin. Christ’s saving work supplies the identity, pardon, power, and hope from which the struggle proceeds.

“Your members which are upon the earth” refers to bodily faculties and inward capacities when surrendered to the rule of sin. The body itself is not evil. It was created by God, assumed by the Son in the incarnation, purchased by Christ, and destined for resurrection. Ascetic mistreatment of the body cannot produce holiness. The command concerns the sinful use of the body and mind—the eyes, imagination, appetite, speech, and actions when they become instruments of unrighteousness.

The severity of “mortify” excludes peaceful coexistence with cherished sin. Temptation must not be entertained, renamed, managed as a harmless habit, or protected as a private entitlement. Sin is to be denied opportunity, starved of cooperation, confessed before God, and resisted through the power of the Spirit. Such mortification may involve fleeing occasions of temptation, removing access, seeking accountability, repairing harm, and repeatedly presenting one’s members to God as instruments of righteousness.

The list moves from outward sexual immorality toward the inward desires that feed it. “Fornication” covers illicit sexual conduct; “uncleanness” points to moral defilement; “inordinate affection” and “evil concupiscence” address disordered passion and desire. Christ’s command reaches beneath behavior to the imagination and will. Sexual holiness protects the dignity of persons by refusing to turn another human being into an object for appetite.

Covetousness gathers up the self-centered hunger running through the list. The covetous heart says that God and His gifts are insufficient and that life depends on possessing more. Desire becomes idolatry when it claims the trust, devotion, and obedience that belong to God alone. Paul therefore presents sanctification as a conflict of worship: sinful desire is overcome not merely by stronger restraint but by a heart increasingly satisfied in Christ and governed by His love.

wordNotes.explanation: The command means to put to death or render powerless. It calls for a decisive repudiation of sinful practices and desires, not physical injury or contempt for the body.
An uncontrolled desire for more—whether possessions, power, pleasure, or another person. It is idolatry because the desired object assumes the place of God in the heart.

verses.bibleText: For which things’ sake the wrath of God cometh on the children of disobedience:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The sins named in verse 5 are serious because they oppose the character and government of God. Divine wrath is not the irritability, vindictiveness, or loss of control associated with sinful human anger. God’s wrath is His holy and judicial response to evil—a response without which love would become indifference toward exploitation, impurity, idolatry, and the destruction these sins produce.

The present wording, “the wrath of God cometh,” points especially toward the coming judgment. God’s patience should not be mistaken for moral approval or inability to act. Evil has an appointed end, and every secret appetite, hidden exploitation, and cherished idol will be brought into judgment. The certainty of that day gives weight to the command to put sin to death now.

Believers are delivered from wrath through Christ, not through moral achievement. His reconciling death provides forgiveness, and His risen life supplies power for renewal. Yet the warning is still addressed to the church because grace must never be distorted into permission for persistent rebellion. The practices listed are not harmless imperfections to be cultivated under a Christian name. A settled refusal to repent reveals allegiance to the old order rather than to Christ.

Judgment according to deeds does not contradict salvation by grace through faith. Deeds cannot purchase salvation, but they disclose what the heart has trusted and served. Living faith bears the fruit of repentance, while persistent disobedience exposes an unchanged loyalty.

The final purpose of divine wrath is the removal of evil from God’s creation. Sin pays its wages in death. Scripture’s last judgment culminates in the second death, when rebellion and its works are brought to their end. God will not perpetuate sin forever; He will vindicate His character, deliver His people, and restore a creation in which righteousness dwells.

wordNotes.explanation: God’s settled and judicial opposition to evil. It is not uncontrolled temper but the necessary response of divine holiness and justice to persistent rebellion.

wordNotes.term: children of disobedience — υἱοὺς τῆς ἀπειθείας (huious tēs apeitheias)
wordNotes.explanation: A Semitic expression describing people whose settled character is marked by refusal to obey God. The phrase is absent from some ancient witnesses but expresses a thought clearly paralleled elsewhere.

verses.bibleText: In the which ye also walked some time, when ye lived in them.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul reminds the Colossians that the vices just named once belonged to their ordinary manner of life. To “walk” in them describes repeated conduct; to “live in them” describes the moral sphere in which that conduct felt natural. Sin was not an occasional interruption of an otherwise holy existence. It shaped desires, customs, relationships, and assumptions before the gospel brought them under the lordship of Christ.

The recollection is meant neither to humiliate forgiven believers nor to encourage fascination with their former lives. It magnifies grace and strengthens the break with sin. They must not return to practices from which Christ has delivered them or treat their past as their permanent identity. The gospel can say truthfully, “such were some of you,” because forgiveness and renewal create a real distinction between what believers once were and what they are becoming.

Remembering the past can also cultivate humility. No Christian stands above those still trapped in sin as though redemption were self-produced. All were dependent on divine mercy. The proper response is gratitude, vigilance, and compassionate witness. A church that remembers the depth of its own deliverance will resist both moral compromise and self-righteous contempt.

wordNotes.explanation: A common biblical metaphor for one’s habitual manner of life and conduct.

verses.bibleText: But now ye also put off all these; anger, wrath, malice, blasphemy, filthy communication out of your mouth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The words “but now” mark the moral change created by the gospel. Former conduct may explain the believers’ history, but it cannot govern their present life. Paul turns from sins of disordered appetite to sins that poison relationships, especially through hostile attitudes and destructive speech. The heavenly life of verses 1-4 must transform not only private desire but also the way members of Christ’s body treat one another.

“Anger” and “wrath” overlap in meaning, though together they can encompass both settled resentment and heated outbursts. “Malice” is the ill will that desires another’s harm or quietly rejoices in it. These inward attitudes commonly find expression through “blasphemy,” which here includes slander, insult, and defamatory speech directed against people, and through shameful communication from the mouth.

The list traces a movement from the heart to the lips. Harsh speech is seldom an isolated accident; it exposes anger, wounded pride, envy, or malice that has been allowed to remain within. Guarding the tongue therefore requires more than replacing offensive words with polite ones. The source must be brought before Christ. Resentment must be confessed, vengeance surrendered, and the offending person viewed as one accountable to God rather than as an object for verbal destruction.

Paul’s command also reaches forms of communication that ancient hearers could not have imagined but that operate by the same moral principles. Anonymous accusation, mocking messages, suggestive humor, manipulated images, public shaming, and the careless repetition of damaging claims all belong under the judgment of this verse. Truth does not require cruelty, and zeal for righteousness does not sanctify contempt.

The imperative “put off” presents these habits as garments inconsistent with the believer’s new identity. They may once have seemed natural, but they no longer fit those who are being renewed in Christ. The speech of the new humanity will later be described as truthful, forgiving, instructive, worshipful, thankful, and governed by the name of Jesus.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to lay aside or remove, sometimes as one removes clothing. It prepares for the garment imagery of putting off the old man and putting on the new.
Shameful, obscene, degrading, or abusive speech. In this context it especially includes language used to dishonor or injure another person.

verses.bibleText: Lie not one to another, seeing that ye have put off the old man with his deeds;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Falsehood is singled out because it makes genuine community impossible. The church has been created by the word of truth and is called to embody that truth in its common life. When believers deceive one another, manipulate facts, conceal wrongdoing, spread what they have not verified, or present a false image of themselves, they attack the trust by which fellowship is sustained.

The prohibition reflects the moral law’s condemnation of false witness. Grace does not weaken that command; it writes truthfulness more deeply into the life of those joined to Christ. The phrase “one to another” emphasizes responsibility within the body, but it does not imply that deception is permissible toward outsiders. Those who represent the God of truth must be trustworthy in every relationship.

Paul grounds the command in a change of clothing: the believers have put off “the old man with his deeds.” The old man is more than a collection of bad habits. It is the former humanity shaped by Adam’s rebellion, governed by sin, and destined for death. Coming to Christ involves a transfer of identity and lordship. The believer no longer belongs to that realm, even though its habits continue to press for renewed expression.

The decisive character of conversion must therefore be joined to continuing obedience. Christians have put off the old man, yet they are commanded to stop wearing his conduct. This is not a contradiction. A new identity has been given in Christ, and daily choices are to become consistent with it. Falsehood belongs to the life that has been renounced.

Truthfulness does not require the reckless disclosure of every private matter, nor does it forbid wise silence when information is not ours to share. It does require that silence never become a disguise for fraud, manipulation, or unrepented harm. The new community speaks truth in love because its members belong to one another under Christ.

wordNotes.explanation: To speak or act falsely with the intention or effect of deceiving. The reciprocal phrase “one to another” highlights the destructive effect of falsehood within the Christian community.

The former humanity identified with Adam, sin, and the old age. The phrase concerns an entire pattern of identity and conduct, not an independent substance within the believer that can be blamed for personal choices.

verses.bibleText:
And have put on the new
man, which is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The change of clothing is completed by putting on “the new man.” This new humanity is found in union with Christ, the true image of God and the head of a reconciled people. Conversion is therefore not merely the improvement of the old life. God brings the believer into a new order whose pattern, power, and destiny are centered in His Son.

The new man “is being renewed.” A decisive transfer has occurred, yet transformation remains progressive. Forgiveness is complete in Christ, but character is not instantly mature. Thought, desire, speech, relationships, and habits must continually be brought into harmony with the identity already received. This protects the passage from two errors: complacency, which assumes that grace leaves conduct unchanged, and perfectionistic self-reliance, which treats sanctification as a human achievement.

The passive form points to God as the One who renews. His Spirit applies the life of Christ, His word exposes falsehood and directs the mind, and His grace enables obedience. Human response remains real: believers are commanded to put off, put on, seek, forgive, love, and obey. Yet every faithful response depends on divine initiative and sustaining power. Sanctification is neither passive indifference nor self-produced righteousness; it is trusting cooperation with the God who works within His people.

Renewal proceeds “in knowledge.” The false teachers apparently promised superior insight through regulations or visionary experience. Paul locates true knowledge in Christ and connects it with moral restoration. To know God is increasingly to perceive His character, recognize His will, reject distorted loyalties, and live truthfully before Him. Knowledge that produces pride, exclusion, or impurity contradicts its claimed source.

The goal is conformity “after the image of him that created him.” The language reaches back to humanity’s creation in God’s image and also to Christ, identified earlier as the image of the invisible God. Sin has disfigured humanity’s reflection of its Creator; Christ reveals what true humanity is and restores that likeness in His people. The renewal begun now will reach its fullness when the redeemed are raised and transformed into His glorious likeness.

wordNotes.explanation: A present passive participle describing an ongoing process of being made new. God is the renewing agent, while believers are called to yield to and participate in His transforming work.
Full or genuine knowledge expressed in recognition of God and conformity to His will. It is relational and moral, not secret information reserved for a spiritual elite.

verses.bibleText:
Where there is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, Barbarian, Scythian, bond
nor free: but Christ
is all, and in all.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The renewal described in verse 10 creates a community in which inherited distinctions can no longer establish spiritual rank. Greek and Jew represent ethnic and cultural division; circumcision and uncircumcision represent religious and covenantal distinction; barbarian and Scythian recall prejudices concerning education and civilization; bond and free expose the deepest legal and social inequality of the ancient household. None of these categories can determine a person’s worth, access to God, standing in the church, or share in salvation.

Paul is not claiming that cultural, familial, or social identities immediately cease to exist. The household instructions beginning in verse 18 acknowledge continuing differences of role and circumstance. Jews remained Jews, Gentiles remained Gentiles, and enslaved believers were still living under oppressive legal conditions. What has been abolished is every claim that such distinctions give one person greater spiritual value or make another less fully a member of Christ.

The reference to Scythians gives the declaration particular force. Ancient writers commonly used the name as an image of extreme cultural inferiority. Paul refuses the contempt built into that stereotype. The gospel is capable of creating a common life between people whom society has trained to fear, despise, exploit, or avoid. A church that reproduces caste, racial superiority, tribal hatred, class contempt, or cultural exclusion denies in practice the new humanity it confesses in doctrine.

The inclusion of “bond nor free” prepares for the instructions concerning slaves and masters. Paul addresses people whose legal status remained radically unequal, yet he declares them equal before Christ and members of the same body. The statement does not make slavery righteous. It introduces principles of brotherhood, shared lordship, inheritance, and impartial judgment that expose the institution’s dehumanizing assumptions.

“Christ is all” means that He replaces every supposed ground of privilege. Heritage, ritual status, education, nationality, wealth, and freedom cannot add to His sufficiency. “And in all” means that the same Christ dwells in every member of His people. It does not teach that all human beings are automatically saved or that Christ is indistinguishable from creation. The context concerns those who have put on the new man. Within that community, Christ supplies the common identity, life, pattern, and hope.

Unity in Christ is therefore neither uniformity nor a polite tolerance that leaves prejudice untouched. It is a new allegiance strong enough to subordinate every lesser identity and create genuine fellowship across boundaries the fallen world treats as absolute.

wordNotes.explanation: “Barbarian” was commonly used by Greek speakers for non-Greek peoples, often with an assumption of cultural inferiority. Scythians were stereotyped in the Greco-Roman world as especially uncivilized or savage. Paul includes even the most despised social categories in the new humanity.

wordNotes.term: Christ is all, and in all — τὰ πάντα καὶ ἐν πᾶσιν Χριστός (ta panta kai en pasin Christos)
wordNotes.explanation: Christ is all-sufficient and supreme within the new humanity, and He dwells in all its members. The statement is neither pantheism nor a claim that every person is automatically united to Christ.

verses.bibleText: Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The negative commands to put away sin are followed by the positive call to put on Christlike character. Christianity cannot be reduced to avoiding prohibited behavior. The old garments must be removed, but the believer must also be clothed with virtues that make the life of Jesus visible within His body.

Identity again precedes command. The Colossians are addressed as “the elect of God, holy and beloved.” These descriptions were used in Scripture for God’s covenant people. Gentile believers need not adopt the false teachers’ rituals to gain a fuller place among the chosen; through Christ they have already been gathered into God’s people. Election is therefore a gift of grace and a summons to holiness, not a ground for superiority or careless presumption. Those whom God has loved and set apart are to display the family likeness of their Father.

“Bowels of mercies” describes compassion that arises from the depth of the person rather than from social obligation. It feels another’s distress and moves toward it with care. Kindness turns that inward compassion into gracious action. Humility abandons the need to secure importance by diminishing others. Meekness is strength governed by love, refusing both self-assertion and retaliation. Longsuffering remains patient when people are slow to change, difficult to understand, or costly to love.

These qualities are particularly necessary in the diverse community described in verse 11. People formed by different cultures, social positions, and histories will misunderstand and offend one another. Unity cannot survive through shared doctrine alone if pride, impatience, and harshness control their relationships. The virtues of verse 12 provide the atmosphere in which truth can be spoken, correction received, and reconciliation pursued.

They also reflect Christ Himself. His compassion welcomed the suffering, His kindness moved toward sinners, His humility led Him to the cross, His meekness refused sinful retaliation, and His patience continues to bear with His people. To put on these virtues is not to construct righteousness independently of Him; it is to allow the life of the One already received to shape the conduct of those who belong to Him.

wordNotes.term: bowels of mercies — σπλάγχνα οἰκτιρμοῦ (splanchna oiktirmou)
wordNotes.explanation: An ancient expression for deep, heartfelt compassion. The KJV’s “bowels” refers to the inward seat of affection and mercy.
A lowly estimate of oneself that refuses self-exaltation and gives thoughtful regard to others. It contrasts with the false humility criticized in Colossians 2:18, 23.

verses.bibleText:
Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also
do ye.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The virtues of verse 12 are tested when genuine grievances arise. Paul assumes that even a renewed community will contain differences, weaknesses, misunderstandings, and real wrongs. Christian fellowship is not sustained by pretending that believers never injure one another. It survives when grace governs the response to those injuries.

Forbearance is the patient willingness to remain in faithful relationship with people whose limitations and habits may be difficult. It resists the impulse to abandon fellowship over every irritation or to demand that others mature according to one’s preferred timetable. Such patience does not treat sin as unimportant; it recognizes that every member of the body is still being renewed.

Forgiveness is required when there is a “quarrel,” or legitimate cause for complaint. The presence of a real grievance makes forgiveness costly. It means relinquishing personal vengeance, refusing to nourish resentment, and declining to use the offense as a permanent weapon against the offender. The standard and enabling ground are found in the words, “even as Christ forgave you.” Believers forgive because they have received mercy for a debt they could never repay, and they forgive in a manner shaped by Christ’s grace.

Forgiveness must not be confused with calling evil good, concealing abuse, removing every consequence, or restoring trust without evidence of change. Scripture can require confrontation, repentance, restitution, discipline, protection of the vulnerable, and truthful testimony. Forbearance is not passive cooperation with continuing violence or manipulation. Forgiveness releases the right of personal retaliation and keeps the heart open to God’s work, while reconciliation ordinarily requires truth and the responsible participation of those involved.

The command also excludes selective forgiveness. Christ’s mercy cannot be gratefully received while bitterness is deliberately preserved as a treasured possession. This does not mean painful feelings disappear immediately. Healing may require time, wise counsel, lament, and strong boundaries. It means that the wounded believer places judgment in God’s hands and refuses to build identity around the injury.

A forgiving church becomes a living witness to the gospel. Its members do not merely announce that reconciliation with God is possible; through costly patience, confession, correction, and mercy, they demonstrate what divine forgiveness creates among human beings.

wordNotes.explanation: To bear with, endure, or make patient room for another person. It acknowledges that fellowship among imperfect people requires sustained grace.
To forgive graciously or freely. The verb is related to charis, “grace,” emphasizing that Christian forgiveness flows from grace already received.

verses.bibleText:
And above all these things
put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Love is pictured as the garment placed over all the virtues already named. It is not a substitute for compassion, holiness, truth, humility, patience, or forgiveness. Rather, it gives them their proper motive and holds them together. Compassion without love can become condescension; truth without love becomes a weapon; patience without love becomes reluctant tolerance; and outward humility without love may conceal a desire for approval.

The word “charity” in the KJV refers to agapē, the self-giving love revealed most clearly in Christ. It is not mere warmth, attraction, or agreement. Love seeks the genuine good of another under the will of God, even when doing so requires sacrifice, correction, endurance, or the surrender of personal advantage. It cannot be separated from holiness, for love rejoices in truth rather than in unrighteousness.

As “the bond of perfectness,” love unites the qualities of Christian character and binds diverse members into mature fellowship. The perfection in view is not self-generated flawlessness but wholeness—character and community brought toward their intended completeness in Christ. Love turns separate virtues into a coherent likeness of Jesus.

The placement of love above all also provides the controlling principle for the household instructions that follow. Submission, authority, obedience, discipline, and labor become distorted when detached from self-giving concern for the other. Wherever love is absent, even formally correct conduct can become harsh, manipulative, or hollow. The new humanity reaches maturity as Christ’s love governs both its convictions and its relationships.

wordNotes.term: bond of perfectness — σύνδεσμος τῆς τελειότητος (syndesmos tēs teleiotētos)
wordNotes.explanation: A bond that joins and carries the other virtues toward mature completeness. The phrase may include both the harmony of Christian character and the unity of the community.

verses.bibleText: And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to the which also ye are called in one body; and be ye thankful.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Love’s unifying work is followed by the command that divine peace govern the heart. The peace in view begins with the reconciliation accomplished through Christ’s blood. Hostility between sinners and God has been answered at the cross, and the same reconciling power is meant to shape relationships among those who have been brought into one body.

The verb translated “rule” carries the picture of an arbiter rendering a decision. When pride, resentment, personal preference, fear, and rivalry compete for control, the peace established by Christ is to be the decisive consideration. This does not mean preserving outward calm at the expense of truth or justice. False peace can protect wrongdoing and silence the wounded. Christ’s peace is grounded in reconciliation through the cross; it faces guilt truthfully, removes hostility through grace, and seeks restored communion in righteousness.

“In your hearts” should not reduce the command to a private feeling used to determine personal guidance. Inner peace can be valuable, but feelings fluctuate and may be mistaken. The plural setting and the reference to “one body” show that Paul is especially concerned with the shared life of the church. The peace of Christ must govern inward attitudes so that it becomes visible in communal decisions, speech, forgiveness, and cooperation.

Believers were called to this peace “in one body.” God’s call does not merely rescue isolated individuals; it joins them to a people. Peace is therefore part of their vocation. A Christian cannot pursue spiritual maturity while treating the unity and welfare of Christ’s body as optional.

“And be ye thankful” is more than an appended courtesy. Gratitude weakens the pride and possessiveness that feed conflict. Those who remember that every spiritual blessing is received by grace are better prepared to forgive, yield personal preference, and rejoice in the gifts of others. Thanksgiving creates soil in which peace can take root without becoming superficial.

wordNotes.term: peace of God — ἡ εἰρήνη τοῦ Χριστοῦ (hē eirēnē tou Christou)
wordNotes.explanation: The KJV reads “peace of God,” while strong ancient textual evidence supports “peace of Christ.” The meanings converge in context: God establishes peace through Christ’s reconciling work.
To act as an arbiter or decisive judge, like an official who settles a contest. Christ’s peace is to become the governing consideration when competing impulses threaten the unity of the body.

verses.bibleText: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The peace of Christ is to rule, and the word of Christ is to dwell. These parallel commands describe a community whose relationships and worship are governed by the same Lord. The “word of Christ” includes both the message about Him and the teaching that carries His authority. It is the apostolic gospel of the divine Son who created all things, became truly human, reconciled sinners through His blood, rose from the dead, reigns above every power, and will appear in glory.

To let this word “dwell in you richly” means more than possessing correct information or hearing an occasional sermon. The plural pronoun points to the church as a whole. Christ’s word must make its home in the congregation—shaping its doctrine, prayers, songs, decisions, counsel, relationships, and response to error. “Richly” excludes a thin familiarity with isolated phrases. The message is to be understood deeply, remembered accurately, applied wisely, and allowed to penetrate the shared life of the body.

Teaching and admonishing belong to the whole community, though not every member exercises the same office. Teaching communicates truth positively; admonishing warns, corrects, and redirects when conduct or belief moves away from Christ. Both require “all wisdom.” Correction without wisdom can humiliate rather than restore, while affection without truth can leave people in danger. Christ-centered wisdom adapts the manner of instruction to the need of the person without altering the truth being taught.

Psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs are included among the means by which believers instruct one another and worship God. The three terms overlap and should not be forced into rigid categories. They encompass the scriptural psalms and other forms of sacred praise shaped by the Spirit and centered on divine truth. Congregational singing is therefore more than emotional preparation or artistic display. It carries theology into memory, gives the community a shared language of faith, warns against error, and strengthens hope.

“Grace in your hearts” may carry the closely related sense of gratitude. The song must arise from hearts conscious of grace rather than from vanity, performance, or competition. Music can be impressive while spiritually empty if its words obscure Christ, contradict Scripture, or direct attention chiefly to the performer. Paul joins truth, wisdom, mutual ministry, heartfelt gratitude, and praise to God.

The parallel with Ephesians 5:18-20 is instructive: there the community is filled with the Spirit; here the word of Christ dwells richly. A Spirit-filled church will be word-filled, and a word-filled church will depend on the Spirit who inspired and applies that word.

wordNotes.term: word of Christ — ὁ λόγος τοῦ Χριστοῦ (ho logos tou Christou)
wordNotes.explanation: The message concerning Christ and proceeding from His authority—the gospel with Christ as its content, center, and interpretive key.
To reside or make a home. The word of Christ is not to visit occasionally but to occupy a settled and abundant place within the community.

verses.bibleText:
And whatsoever ye do in word or deed,
do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God and the Father by him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The verse gathers the preceding exhortations into an all-embracing principle. “Whatsoever ye do” leaves no protected territory in which Christ’s authority may be ignored. Speech and action represent the two great outward expressions of life, and both are to be brought under the name of the Lord Jesus.

Acting in His name is not merely saying His name before or after an activity. It means acting as one who belongs to Him, bears His reputation, submits to His command, reflects His character, and seeks His glory. A believer should be able to place every word, transaction, relationship, form of entertainment, act of service, and private decision beneath Christ’s lordship. Anything that cannot truthfully be associated with His holy name must be refused.

This principle removes the artificial division between sacred and ordinary life. Worship, household responsibilities, employment, hospitality, study, rest, and conversation may all become service to Christ. Their spiritual value does not depend on public visibility but on faithfulness to Him. Conversely, an activity commonly regarded as religious is not acceptable merely because it occurs in a church setting; it too must agree with the truth and character of Jesus.

Thanksgiving again accompanies obedience. Christian conduct is not the anxious labor of people trying to earn divine acceptance. It is the grateful response of those reconciled through Christ. Thanks are directed to God the Father “by him,” acknowledging that access, worship, and every saving blessing come through the Son. The full deity of Christ is not weakened by this mediatorial role; the eternal Son became truly human and stands as the sufficient mediator through whom redeemed humanity approaches the Father.

Verse 17 also prepares for the household instructions. Marriage, parenting, obedience, and labor are not separate from the heavenly life. Each must be conducted in the name of Jesus and tested by His lordship.

wordNotes.term: in the name of the Lord Jesus — ἐν ὀνόματι κυρίου Ἰησοῦ (en onomati kyriou Iēsou)
wordNotes.explanation: To act under Jesus’ authority, in harmony with His character, as His representative, and for His honor. It is more than attaching a verbal formula to an action.

verses.bibleText: Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as it is fit in the Lord.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The general command to do everything in the name of Jesus is now applied to the household. Greco-Roman discussions commonly treated the home through three relationships: wife and husband, child and father, slave and master. Such discussions ordinarily centered on the authority of the male head. Paul addresses each party directly as a responsible member of the Christian assembly and places every relationship beneath the lordship of Christ.

The wife is called to submit to her husband. Submission does not declare women intellectually, morally, or spiritually inferior. Verse 11 has already removed social distinctions as grounds of worth and privilege in the new humanity. Husband and wife share creation in God’s image, redemption in Christ, access to God, and hope of the inheritance. Nor is submission identical with the obedience required of children and slaves; Paul deliberately uses different language.

Within marriage, submission describes a willing recognition of covenantal order rather than coerced servitude. The command is addressed to wives as moral agents. It is not handed to husbands as a weapon by which they may demand compliance, silence questions, control conscience, or excuse domination. The following command places the husband under the searching obligation of self-giving love and forbids harshness.

“As it is fit in the Lord” gives the instruction its distinctly Christian setting. The wife’s relation to her husband is governed by her prior and supreme allegiance to Christ. No human authority is absolute, and no command to sin carries divine obligation. Submission cannot require participation in wrongdoing, concealment of abuse, abandonment of truth, or passive endurance of violence. Seeking safety, counsel, protection, or lawful intervention does not violate allegiance to the Lord.

The phrase also means that submission should express the character of life in Christ—freely, wisely, respectfully, and without servile fear. Marriage is not a contest for personal sovereignty but a one-flesh covenant in which both persons seek the other’s good under God. The husband’s leadership, where exercised according to the wider apostolic teaching, must resemble Christ’s sacrificial care rather than the self-protective power patterns of the fallen world.

Paul works within the household structures known to his hearers while placing within them a transforming principle: Jesus, not custom, pride, or the paterfamilias, is Lord. Every form of order must therefore be judged by His truth, holiness, justice, and self-giving love.

wordNotes.explanation: To place oneself within an ordered relationship. The form and context indicate willing submission rather than forced subjugation, and Paul uses a different verb from the command for children and slaves to obey.

wordNotes.term: as it is fit — ὡς ἀνῆκεν (hōs anēken)
wordNotes.explanation: As is proper or fitting for those whose life is lived in the sphere of the Lord. Christ defines both the character and limits of the relationship.

verses.bibleText:
Husbands, love
your wives, and be not bitter against them.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The husband’s responsibility is expressed first by love and then by the rejection of bitterness. In the surrounding culture, household instruction generally emphasized a husband’s right to govern and preserve order. Paul emphasizes the character with which he must relate to his wife. Authority is not enlarged; it is placed beneath the demanding measure of self-giving love.

The command is continuous: husbands are to keep loving their wives. This love is more than affection or sexual attraction, though both may properly belong to marriage. It is the deliberate pursuit of the wife’s welfare, dignity, holiness, security, and joy. The fuller parallel in Ephesians points to Christ, who gave Himself for the church. Any claim to Christian leadership that protects male privilege while sacrificing the wife’s wellbeing reverses the pattern of Jesus.

“Be not bitter against them” addresses both the inward attitude and its outward expression. Resentment may arise when expectations are disappointed, preferences are challenged, or a husband believes his position entitles him to unquestioned service. If cherished, bitterness appears as cold withdrawal, contempt, ridicule, intimidation, manipulation, sexual coercion, angry speech, or physical violence. Every such expression contradicts the command to love.

The verse leaves no room for harsh patriarchy baptized with religious language. A husband cannot use verse 18 to demand what verse 19 forbids him to become. Love listens, honors, protects, repents when wrong, and often yields personal preference for the good of the wife. It treats her not as household property or an assistant to his ambitions but as one who shares God’s image and the grace of life.

Christlike love also seeks reconciliation without denying truth. It is patient and kind, yet it does not manipulate with apparent kindness or avoid necessary confession. The husband’s responsibility is measured not by how firmly he asserts authority but by how faithfully his conduct reflects the crucified Lord.

wordNotes.explanation: A continuing command to practice self-giving love that seeks the wife’s true good. Christ’s sacrificial love supplies the governing pattern.

wordNotes.term: be not bitter — μὴ πικραίνεσθε (mē pikrainesthe)
wordNotes.explanation: Do not become embittered or act harshly. The expression includes resentful attitudes and the severe, domineering treatment that flows from them.

verses.bibleText:
Children, obey
your parents in all things: for this is well pleasing unto the Lord.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Children are addressed directly, suggesting that they were present as responsible participants when the letter was read to the congregation. They are not treated merely as possessions managed by the father. Christ claims their allegiance and gives them a meaningful place within the moral life of the household.

Obedience gives practical expression to the commandment to honor father and mother. Young people living under parental care are ordinarily to heed instruction, respect household order, and accept appropriate correction. Such obedience trains the will, protects from dangers not yet fully understood, and contributes to the peace of the home.

“In all things” expresses the comprehensive character of ordinary obedience, but it cannot make parental authority absolute. The reason given is that such conduct is well pleasing “unto the Lord,” or, according to a strongly attested reading, “in the Lord.” The child’s highest allegiance remains with Christ. A parental demand to lie, steal, conceal abuse, reject God’s command, or participate in any other sin carries no divine obligation. Human authority is valid only beneath God’s authority.

The principle also changes as children mature and establish households of their own. Lifelong honor, gratitude, and appropriate care remain, while the direct obedience expected of a dependent child does not necessarily continue unchanged into adulthood.

Parents should notice that obedience is described in relation to the Lord, not merely to parental convenience. Children are not called to exist as extensions of a parent’s reputation or ambition. Their obedience is part of their own discipleship, and parental guidance should help them develop an intelligent, willing allegiance to Christ.

wordNotes.explanation: To heed and comply with rightful instruction. In the household setting it describes the ordinary responsibility of children under parental care and authority.

verses.bibleText:
Fathers, provoke not your children
to anger, lest they be discouraged.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Parental authority is immediately placed under restraint. Children must obey, but fathers must not exercise authority in a way that crushes the child’s spirit. In the Roman household the father possessed extensive legal and social power. Paul directs attention not toward enlarging that power but toward the danger of misusing it.

Provocation may take many forms: continual criticism, humiliation, unpredictable anger, favoritism, impossible expectations, public comparison, refusal to listen, punishment disconnected from instruction, or the withholding of affection until performance satisfies the parent. Even well-intended demands can become destructive when the child hears only disapproval and never receives patient guidance or hope.

The stated danger is that children become “discouraged”—they lose heart and conclude that obedience, growth, or parental acceptance is unattainable. Discipline intended to form character can then produce secrecy, resentment, despair, or outward compliance without inward trust. A parent may win immediate submission while weakening the child’s willingness to pursue what is good.

The verse does not forbid correction. Biblical discipline is purposeful, proportionate, consistent, and directed toward restoration. It distinguishes immaturity from defiance, explains rather than merely punishes, and joins firmness with affection. God’s fatherly discipline supplies the pattern: He corrects those He loves for their good, understands their weakness, and does not treat them according to uncontrolled anger.

Although “fathers” reflects the person who normally held household authority in Paul’s setting, the moral principle applies to every parent or guardian. Authority should help children grow toward mature responsibility before God. The goal is not to reproduce the parent’s personality or ambitions but to nurture courage, truthfulness, wisdom, and faith in Christ.

wordNotes.explanation: To stir up or provoke a reaction. Here it describes parental conduct that repeatedly irritates, exasperates, or drives a child toward resentment.
To lose heart, become dispirited, or give up. This is the only New Testament occurrence of the verb.

verses.bibleText:
Servants, obey in all things
your masters according to the flesh; not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but in singleness of heart, fearing God:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The KJV’s “servants” translates a term that ordinarily means slaves. Historical honesty requires retaining that reality. Roman slavery took varied forms, and some enslaved people possessed education, responsibility, or prospects of release, but they remained legally owned and vulnerable to coercion, sale, punishment, and family separation. The relationship cannot simply be equated with modern employment.

Paul addresses enslaved believers within an institution he neither created nor explicitly endorses here. His purpose is to instruct Christians living under an existing social order. The absence of an immediate command for universal emancipation should not be turned into divine approval of human ownership. Verse 11 has already declared that slave and free possess equal standing in the new humanity, Philemon is urged to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother, and Colossians 4:1 will place masters under the authority of a heavenly Master. These principles undermine the claim that one person may possess another as an inferior kind of being.

The direct address itself is significant. Slaves are present within the worshipping community and are treated as morally responsible disciples rather than as household equipment. Their earthly condition does not prevent Christ from claiming their conscience, receiving their service, or promising them an inheritance.

“Masters according to the flesh” limits the sphere of human mastery. These masters possess authority only within the present earthly order; they cannot rule the conscience, determine eternal identity, or replace the lordship of Christ. Consequently, obedience can never require idolatry, denial of Christ, or participation in sin. The broader biblical principle remains: God must be obeyed above human authority.

Paul condemns “eyeservice,” labor performed diligently only when the owner is watching, and the conduct of “menpleasers,” whose concern is appearance and advantage rather than integrity. He calls instead for singleness of heart. The enslaved believer’s inward freedom allows conduct to be governed by reverence for God rather than by constant calculation of what can be concealed from an earthly master.

This exhortation does not excuse exploitation or tell oppressed people that injustice is unimportant. Masters are accountable to the same Lord, and verse 25 warns of impartial judgment. Nor does faithful service mean that an enslaved person must refuse a lawful opportunity for freedom; Paul elsewhere says that freedom should be used when it becomes available.

The principles of sincerity, diligence, and service to Christ may be applied secondarily to employment, but the original setting must not disappear. Employees ordinarily possess rights and freedom of movement that slaves lacked. Application should therefore include not only responsible work but also the obligation of employers to reject coercion, exploitation, unsafe conditions, withheld wages, and every practice that treats workers as disposable property.

wordNotes.explanation: Service performed only while being watched. The rare compound exposes conduct aimed at appearance rather than genuine faithfulness.

wordNotes.term: singleness of heart — ἁπλότης καρδίας (haplotēs kardias)
wordNotes.explanation: Sincerity, integrity, and undivided purpose—the opposite of hypocritical service designed merely to gain human approval.

verses.bibleText:
And whatsoever ye do, do
it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The comprehensive “whatsoever ye do” echoes verse 17 and applies its principle particularly to enslaved believers. Work that earthly society regarded as menial or invisible could be offered to Christ. Its dignity did not depend on the social honor attached to the task but on the Lord to whom it was ultimately rendered.

To work “heartily” means to act from the whole inner person. Paul is not romanticizing forced labor or demanding artificial enthusiasm about oppression. He calls for integrity that cannot be reduced to supervision. Even when human recognition is absent, the believer remains conscious of Christ’s presence and authority.

“As to the Lord, and not unto men” changes the deepest motive without denying the immediate human relationship. The earthly master may receive the result of the labor, but Christ receives the believer’s faithfulness. Human beings can overlook, exploit, or misjudge service; the Lord sees its true character.

The command cannot make an immoral task righteous. Service to Christ excludes participation in fraud, cruelty, idolatry, sexual exploitation, or any act contrary to His will. Neither can the verse be used by those in power to demand unlimited labor while ignoring justice. The Lord who sees the worker also judges the person who controls the conditions of work.

For Christians in every form of honest vocation, the principle removes the division between visible ministry and ordinary responsibility. Faithfulness in unnoticed duties, careful craftsmanship, truthful administration, and service to vulnerable people can become worship when performed under Christ’s lordship.

wordNotes.explanation: Literally, “from the soul,” meaning from the whole inner person, with sincerity and undivided purpose.

verses.bibleText: Knowing that of the Lord ye shall receive the reward of the inheritance: for ye serve the Lord Christ.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The promise of an inheritance would have sounded extraordinary to enslaved hearers. Under ordinary social arrangements, a slave could be treated as part of another person’s estate rather than as an heir. In Christ, those denied earthly standing are promised the same eternal inheritance as free believers and masters. Social rank cannot diminish their place among God’s children.

The inheritance gathers up the promises of salvation, resurrection, the kingdom, and life in the restored creation. It is presently kept secure with God and will be openly received when Christ appears. The promise does not shift Christian hope toward a conscious, disembodied reward at death. The chapter has already located the manifestation of glory at Christ’s appearing, when the redeemed share His victory through resurrection and transformation.

Calling the inheritance a “reward” does not mean eternal life is earned as wages. Scripture presents the inheritance as a gift secured through Christ and received by grace. Faithful service is nevertheless remembered and openly acknowledged by God. The obedience of faith is not the purchase price of salvation; it is the fruit of belonging to the Lord and the evidence of the allegiance His grace has created.

The promise also answers the injustice of earthly masters. A slave’s work might be ignored, underpaid, or forcibly taken, but Christ cannot be deprived of the ability to reward His servant. He judges with perfect knowledge of motive, opportunity, suffering, and faithfulness.

“Ye serve the Lord Christ” declares the controlling reality of the passage. The earthly master is not ultimate. Jesus, the crucified and risen Messiah, is Lord over slave and free alike. Read as a command, the words summon the believer to serve Him; read as a statement, they identify whom the believer is already serving. In either case, Christ’s lordship gives dignity to the oppressed and accountability to every person who exercises power.

wordNotes.term: reward of the inheritance — ἀνταπόδοσιν τῆς κληρονομίας (antapodosin tēs klēronomias)
wordNotes.explanation: The recompense consisting in the promised inheritance. The language is striking for slaves, who ordinarily possessed little expectation of receiving an earthly inheritance.

wordNotes.term: the Lord Christ — τῷ κυρίῳ Χριστῷ (tō kyriō Christō)
wordNotes.explanation: An emphatic designation identifying Jesus Christ as the believer’s true Master. The final clause may be read as either a statement, “ye serve the Lord Christ,” or an imperative, “serve the Lord Christ.”

verses.bibleText: But he that doeth wrong shall receive for the wrong which he hath done: and there is no respect of persons.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The promise of reward is balanced by a warning of judgment. Union with Christ cannot be used as a shield for wrongdoing. The enslaved believer is morally responsible before God, and the socially powerful master cannot assume that rank will protect him. The wording looks back to the servants just addressed and forward toward the command to masters in Colossians 4:1. Its principle embraces both.

“He that doeth wrong shall receive for the wrong which he hath done” affirms the moral seriousness of human conduct. God sees injuries hidden by household power, economic dependence, reputation, or fear. The wrongdoer may escape human investigation, manipulate the legal system, or compel the injured person’s silence, but no injustice disappears from the knowledge of the Lord.

The warning is especially powerful in a society where masters possessed advantages before the law and slaves were easily treated as less credible or less valuable. God receives no person’s “face.” He is not impressed by title, freedom, education, wealth, ethnicity, religious reputation, or public influence. The master and the slave stand before the same Judge.

Judgment according to deeds must remain connected to the gospel of grace. Human works do not create a claim upon salvation, and no quantity of obedience can replace Christ’s righteousness or atoning death. Deeds nevertheless reveal the direction of the life. They bear witness to whether faith has received Christ’s transforming lordship or whether the person has continued to serve self and sin while merely professing His name.

This impartial judgment brings both warning and consolation. It warns every believer against secret wrongdoing, exploitation, laziness, deception, and abuse of authority. It consoles those whose suffering has never been acknowledged on earth. God’s judgment will expose evil, vindicate His character, and set right what human courts and households have left unresolved.

The recompense of unrepented evil is not endless preservation in sin but the death toward which sin leads. God’s final judgment removes rebellion from His creation, while those whose life is hidden with Christ receive the promised inheritance at His appearing. The chapter thus ends where it began: every earthly relationship must be lived beneath the throne of the risen Lord.

wordNotes.explanation: To receive back or obtain what is due. In this setting it points toward divine recompense in the final judgment.
Partiality based on outward status—literally, the receiving of a face. God’s judgment cannot be influenced by rank, wealth, freedom, ethnicity, or power.
